title: Turning the Tide: How ASEAN Is Building a Regional Response to Plastic Pollution

image.alt: Plastic waste and debris floating underwater

excerpt: Delegates from all ten ASEAN member states endorsed a shared commitment to coordinated action on marine litter, marking a turning point for Southeast Asia's approach to ocean plastics.

body.text: When ASEAN leaders convened in Bangkok in 2019, marine litter was no longer a fringe concern — it had become a regional priority. Delegates from all ten member states endorsed a shared commitment to coordinated action, marking a turning point for Southeast Asia's approach to ocean plastics.

That commitment became the ASEAN Regional Framework on Marine Debris — a strategic blueprint designed to align national efforts under a common set of goals. While each country faces distinct challenges, the framework provides a shared language and accountability structure for collective progress.

body.alt: Volunteers in red shirts collecting plastic waste on a beach
body.caption: Volunteers sort collected waste during a coastal cleanup in Sulawesi, Indonesia.

body.text: Across the region, several countries have made meaningful strides. Indonesia and Thailand have invested heavily in waste-collection infrastructure. The Philippines has pioneered community-led recovery programs. Vietnam is scaling up recycling capacity in its industrial zones. Yet significant gaps remain — fragmented data systems, underfunded enforcement, and limited private-sector engagement continue to slow progress.

items: Shifting toward a circular economy that reduces plastic production and consumption at the source;
Strengthening waste-management infrastructure to stop leakage before it reaches waterways;
Scaling public-private partnerships that bring investment and innovation to waste recovery;

body.text: Cross-sector collaboration — between governments, researchers, civil society, and the private sector — is essential to close the gap between policy ambition and on-the-ground results.

Marine plastic pollution is not just an environmental crisis. It threatens fisheries and tourism, degrades coastal ecosystems, and poses direct risks to human health through microplastic contamination. For ASEAN, a region with some of the world's most biodiverse coastlines, the stakes are uniquely high — and the window for meaningful action is narrowing.

title: World Bank Backs New Plastic Circular Economy Fund for Southeast Asia

image.alt: Workers sorting recyclable plastic at a materials recovery facility

excerpt: A new blended-finance fund will support recycling infrastructure and waste-collection enterprises across the region.

body.text: The fund is designed to close the financing gap for small and medium recycling enterprises, which collect and process the majority of the region's post-consumer plastic waste.
Grants and concessional loans will be channelled through local financial institutions, prioritising waste-collection cooperatives and women-led recycling businesses.

title: Training Programme Equips Coastal Communities to Track Local Plastic Sources

image.alt: Community members participating in a waste-audit training session

excerpt: Over 200 community volunteers have been trained to conduct waste audits and identify local pollution hotspots.

body.text: The programme pairs local volunteers with environmental scientists to conduct brand and source audits, helping municipalities target interventions where they will have the greatest impact.
